title: Reproduction (Plant & Human)
description: How plants and humans reproduce — flower structure, pollination, fertilisation, seed dispersal, human reproductive systems, puberty, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and birth.

notes.heading: Flower Structure and Pollination
notes.body: A flower is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant (angiosperm). Key parts: Petals — often brightly coloured to attract insect pollinators. Sepals — green, leaf-like structures protecting the flower bud. Stamen (male part) — consists of the anther (produces pollen grains containing male gametes) and the filament (stalk supporting the anther). Carpel/Pistil (female part) — consists of the stigma (sticky top that catches pollen), the style (tube connecting stigma to ovary), and the ovary (contains ovules, each with a female gamete/egg cell). Nectary — produces sugary nectar to attract pollinators. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same species. Cross-pollination (between different plants) is preferred because it increases genetic variation. Self-pollination (same flower/plant) can occur but reduces variation. Insect-pollinated flowers: large, colourful petals; scented; produce nectar; sticky, spiky pollen grains (to attach to insects); stigma inside flower (insect brushes past). Wind-pollinated flowers: small, dull petals (often green); no scent/nectar; anthers hang outside flower (exposed to wind); produce huge amounts of light, smooth pollen; feathery stigma outside flower (to catch airborne pollen).

illustration.alt: Labelled cross-section of an insect-pollinated flower showing petals, sepals, stamen, carpel and ovules.
illustration.caption: The flower contains male stamens and a female carpel; petals and nectar attract pollinators.

notes.heading: Fertilisation, Seed Formation and Dispersal
notes.body: After pollination, a pollen grain on the stigma germinates: it grows a pollen tube down through the style, digesting its way through the tissue. The male gamete (nucleus) travels down the pollen tube to reach an ovule in the ovary. Fertilisation: the male gamete fuses with the female gamete (egg cell) inside the ovule, forming a zygote. The zygote develops into an embryo (the baby plant). The ovule develops into a seed. The ovary develops into a fruit. The seed contains: the embryo (future plant), a food store (cotyledons — for energy during germination), and a protective seed coat (testa). Fruits are adapted for seed dispersal: (1) Wind dispersal — light seeds with wings or parachutes (e.g., dandelion, sycamore). (2) Animal dispersal (internal) — seeds in fleshy, colourful fruits; animals eat fruit, seeds pass through digestive system unharmed and are deposited in faeces (e.g., berries, apple). (3) Animal dispersal (external) — seeds with hooks or barbs that catch on animal fur (e.g., burdock). (4) Water dispersal — buoyant, waterproof seeds (e.g., coconut). (5) Explosive/mechanical dispersal — pods that dry and split, flinging seeds out (e.g., pea pods, lupins). Dispersal reduces competition between parent plant and offspring for light, water, and nutrients.

illustration.alt: Diagram of pollen-tube fertilisation, seed and fruit formation, and five seed-dispersal methods.
illustration.caption: Fertilisation creates a zygote inside the ovule; fruits and seeds are adapted for wind, animal, water or explosive dispersal.

notes.heading: Germination
notes.body: Germination is the process by which a seed develops into a new plant. The seed must be viable (alive) and not dormant. Three conditions are required: (1) Water — activates enzymes that break down the food store in the cotyledon; softens the seed coat. (2) Oxygen — needed for aerobic respiration to provide energy for growth. (3) Warmth — optimum temperature for enzyme activity. Light is NOT needed for germination (seeds often germinate underground). The process: (1) Seed absorbs water and swells. (2) Enzymes break down stored starch in the cotyledon into glucose. (3) Glucose is respired to produce ATP energy. (4) The radicle (embryonic root) emerges first, growing downwards (positive gravitropism). (5) The plumule (embryonic shoot) emerges later, growing upwards (negative gravitropism). (6) Once the plumule reaches light, the seedling begins photosynthesising and no longer relies on the food store. Practical: investigate germination conditions by setting up test tubes with cress seeds — vary water, oxygen (use boiled water/oil layer), or temperature — and observe which germinate.

illustration.alt: Four-stage diagram of seed germination from dry seed to photosynthesising seedling.
illustration.caption: Water, oxygen and warmth trigger germination: the radicle grows down first, then the plumule grows up.

notes.heading: Human Male Reproductive System
notes.body: The male reproductive system produces and delivers sperm. Key organs: Testes (singular: testis) — pair of organs hanging outside the body in the scrotum. This external position keeps them 2-3°C cooler than body temperature, which is essential for sperm production (spermatogenesis). The testes also produce the hormone testosterone. Sperm duct (vas deferens) — tube carrying sperm from each testis to the urethra. Glands (seminal vesicles and prostate gland) — add fluids to sperm to form semen. This fluid contains nutrients (fructose) for energy and is alkaline to neutralise the acidic environment of the vagina. Urethra — tube running through the centre of the penis; carries either semen or urine (never both simultaneously — a valve prevents mixing). Penis — organ that delivers sperm into the female's vagina during sexual intercourse; contains erectile tissue that fills with blood to become erect. A sperm cell is highly specialised: head contains the nucleus (23 chromosomes — haploid) and an acrosome (enzyme cap for penetrating the egg); midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy; tail (flagellum) for swimming.

illustration.alt: Labelled diagram of the male reproductive system and an inset of a sperm cell.
illustration.caption: Sperm are produced in the testes at a temperature 2-3 °C below body temperature, then travel through ducts and glands.

notes.heading: Human Female Reproductive System
notes.body: The female reproductive system produces eggs, receives sperm, and nurtures the developing baby. Key organs: Ovaries — pair of organs producing and releasing eggs (ova). At birth, a female already has all the immature egg cells she will ever have (~1-2 million). From puberty, approximately one egg matures and is released each month (ovulation). Ovaries also produce the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. Oviducts (fallopian tubes) — tubes connecting ovaries to the uterus. Fertilisation normally occurs here. The inner lining has cilia that waft the egg (or embryo) towards the uterus. Uterus (womb) — muscular organ where a fertilised egg implants and the embryo develops. The lining (endometrium) thickens with blood-rich tissue each month in preparation for pregnancy. Cervix — a ring of muscle at the base of the uterus, keeping the foetus in place during pregnancy. Vagina — muscular tube receiving sperm during intercourse; also the birth canal through which the baby is delivered. An egg cell (ovum) is one of the largest human cells, containing cytoplasm with nutrients to support early development.

illustration.alt: Labelled diagram of the female reproductive system and an inset of an egg cell.
illustration.caption: Eggs mature in the ovaries, travel through the oviducts, and the uterus lining thickens ready for implantation.

notes.heading: Puberty and the Menstrual Cycle
notes.body: Puberty is the period of physical changes through which a child's body becomes capable of sexual reproduction. Triggered by hormones (testosterone in males, oestrogen in females). Male changes (ages ~10-15): voice deepens, shoulders broaden, facial and body hair grows, testes and penis enlarge, sperm production begins, growth spurt. Female changes (ages ~9-14): breasts develop, hips widen, body hair grows, menstrual cycle begins (menarche), growth spurt. Both sexes: pubic hair, acne (due to increased oil production), emotional changes. The menstrual cycle (approximately 28 days) prepares the female body for potential pregnancy each month: Days 1-5 — Menstruation: the thickened uterus lining breaks down and is shed (a period) if no fertilised egg has implanted. Days 5-14 — The lining rebuilds, thickening with blood vessels. Oestrogen levels rise. Day 14 (approximately) — Ovulation: an egg is released from an ovary into the oviduct. Days 14-28 — Progesterone maintains the thickened lining. If fertilisation does not occur, progesterone drops, triggering the next period. If fertilisation does occur, the lining is maintained. Key hormones: FSH (from pituitary) — stimulates egg maturation; Oestrogen (from ovaries) — rebuilds uterine lining; LH (from pituitary) — triggers ovulation; Progesterone (from ovary/placenta) — maintains lining.

illustration.alt: Diagram of the 28-day menstrual cycle showing uterus lining changes, ovulation and hormone levels.
illustration.caption: The cycle rebuilds and maintains the uterus lining; if no fertilised egg implants, the lining is shed.

notes.heading: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Birth
notes.body: Fertilisation: During sexual intercourse, semen is ejaculated into the vagina. Millions of sperm swim through the cervix, into the uterus, and into the oviducts. Only a few hundred reach the egg. One sperm penetrates the egg's outer layer; their nuclei fuse to form a zygote with the full 46 chromosomes (23 from each parent). The fertilised egg immediately forms a barrier preventing other sperm from entering. Pregnancy: The zygote divides by mitosis as it travels down the oviduct, forming a ball of cells (embryo). After about 5-7 days, the embryo implants into the thickened uterine lining (endometrium). The placenta develops — a disc-shaped organ embedding into the uterine wall, connected to the foetus by the umbilical cord. The placenta allows exchange between maternal and foetal blood (which never mix): oxygen and nutrients (glucose, amino acids) diffuse from mother to foetus; waste (CO₂, urea) diffuses from foetus to mother to be excreted. The placenta also produces progesterone to maintain the pregnancy. The amnion (amniotic sac) surrounds the foetus, filled with amniotic fluid that cushions and protects against impacts. Gestation is approximately 40 weeks (9 months). Birth: The cervix dilates, the amniotic sac ruptures ('waters break'), and powerful uterine contractions push the baby through the cervix and vagina. After birth, the placenta (afterbirth) is delivered.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing fertilisation in the oviduct, implantation, and the placenta and amniotic sac during pregnancy.
illustration.caption: Sperm fertilise the egg in the oviduct; the embryo implants in the uterus and exchanges substances via the placenta.

flashcards.definition: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same species.
flashcards.example: Bees carry pollen between flowers as they collect nectar — an example of insect pollination.

flashcards.definition: The fusion of a male gamete (from pollen) with a female gamete (egg cell in ovule) to form a zygote, which develops into an embryo inside a seed.
flashcards.example: The pollen tube grows down the style and delivers the male nucleus to the ovule.

flashcards.definition: The male reproductive part of a flower, consisting of the anther (produces pollen) and filament (stalk).
flashcards.example: Lily flowers have prominent stamens with large anthers covered in orange pollen.

flashcards.definition: The female reproductive part of a flower, consisting of the stigma (catches pollen), style, and ovary (contains ovules).
flashcards.example: The sticky stigma at the top of the carpel receives and holds pollen grains.

flashcards.definition: The movement of seeds away from the parent plant, reducing competition and enabling colonisation of new areas. Methods: wind, animal, water, explosive.
flashcards.example: Dandelion seeds have parachute-like structures for wind dispersal; coconuts float for water dispersal.

flashcards.definition: Male reproductive organs producing sperm (by meiosis) and the hormone testosterone. Located in the scrotum, outside the body for temperature control.
flashcards.example: Sperm production requires a temperature ~35°C, which is 2-3°C below normal body temperature.

flashcards.definition: Female reproductive organs containing immature egg cells. From puberty, one egg matures and is released approximately each month (ovulation). Produce oestrogen and progesterone.
flashcards.example: At birth, ovaries contain ~1-2 million immature eggs; only about 400-500 will be ovulated in a lifetime.

flashcards.definition: The release of a mature egg (ovum) from an ovary into the oviduct, occurring approximately day 14 of a 28-day menstrual cycle.
flashcards.example: Fertilisation is most likely if intercourse occurs in the days around ovulation.

flashcards.definition: The monthly shedding of the thickened uterus lining (endometrium) through the vagina when no fertilised egg has implanted. Days 1-5 of the cycle.
flashcards.example: A period (menstruation) marks the beginning of each menstrual cycle.

flashcards.definition: Disc-shaped organ embedding into the uterine wall during pregnancy; allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste between mother and foetus via diffusion. Maternal and foetal blood do NOT mix.
flashcards.example: Harmful substances (alcohol, nicotine, some drugs) can cross the placenta and damage the developing foetus.

flashcards.definition: Liquid filling the amniotic sac surrounding the developing foetus; cushions and protects against mechanical shock and allows the foetus to move.
flashcards.example: The 'waters breaking' at the start of labour is the rupture of the amniotic sac.

flashcards.definition: The single cell formed when the nuclei of a sperm and egg fuse during fertilisation; contains the full 46 chromosomes (diploid).
flashcards.example: The zygote divides by mitosis into 2, 4, 8, 16... cells as it travels to the uterus for implantation.

questions.stem: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
questions.explanation: The anther, part of the stamen (male reproductive organ), produces pollen grains containing the male gametes.

questions.stem: A flower has small, dull green petals, no scent, and feathery stigmas hanging outside. How is it most likely pollinated?
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers are typically small and dull (no need to attract insects), with exposed feathery stigmas to catch airborne pollen and large amounts of light, smooth pollen.

questions.stem: After pollination, the pollen grain grows a tube down through the style. What is this tube's purpose?
choices: To deliver the male gamete nucleus to the ovule for fertilisation
To anchor the flower more firmly
questions.explanation: The pollen tube digests its way through the style tissue to deliver the male gamete to the ovule, where fertilisation occurs.

questions.stem: Which part of the flower develops into the fruit after fertilisation?
questions.explanation: After fertilisation, the ovary wall develops into the fruit, while the ovules inside develop into seeds.

questions.stem: Why is seed dispersal important for plants?
choices: It prevents the seed from germinating too early
It reduces competition with the parent plant for light, water, and nutrients, and allows colonisation of new areas
It helps the seed absorb more water
questions.explanation: If all seeds fell directly under the parent plant, seedlings would compete with each other and the parent. Dispersal spreads offspring to new locations with potentially better conditions.

questions.stem: Which three conditions are required for seed germination?
questions.explanation: Water activates enzymes and softens the seed coat; oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration to release energy; warmth provides the optimum temperature for enzyme activity. Light is NOT needed — seeds often germinate underground.

questions.stem: Why are the testes located outside the body in the scrotum?
choices: To protect them from injury inside the body
To keep them 2-3°C cooler than body temperature, which is essential for sperm production
To make them more visible as a sign of puberty
To allow them to move closer to the penis
questions.explanation: Sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires a temperature slightly below normal body temperature. The external location of the testes maintains this optimum temperature.

questions.stem: In which part of the female reproductive system does fertilisation normally occur?
questions.explanation: Sperm swim through the uterus and meet the egg in the oviduct. The fertilised egg (zygote) then travels down the oviduct to implant in the uterus.

questions.stem: On approximately which day of a 28-day menstrual cycle does ovulation occur?
questions.explanation: Ovulation — the release of a mature egg from the ovary — typically occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle, triggered by a surge in LH (luteinising hormone).

questions.stem: What is the function of the placenta during pregnancy?
choices: It allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste between mother and foetus without their blood mixing
It stores food for the foetus to eat
questions.explanation: The placenta is the site of diffusion between maternal and foetal blood — oxygen and nutrients move to the foetus; CO₂ and urea move to the mother for excretion. The blood supplies do NOT mix.

questions.stem: Why does the uterus lining (endometrium) thicken during the menstrual cycle?
choices: To provide extra space for the ovaries to grow
To prepare a rich, blood-filled surface for a fertilised egg to implant into
To push the egg into the oviduct
To produce more eggs for fertilisation
questions.explanation: The endometrium thickens with blood vessels each cycle to create a nourishing environment for a potential embryo. If no fertilisation occurs, it is shed during menstruation.

questions.stem: A student investigates germination by placing cress seeds in four test tubes: A — water, oxygen, 20°C; B — no water, oxygen, 20°C; C — water, no oxygen (boiled water + oil layer), 20°C; D — water, oxygen, 4°C. Which seeds will germinate?
choices: A only — it provides all three conditions (water, oxygen, warmth)
A and D only — water is the most important factor
All of them — seeds always germinate eventually
A, B, and C — temperature is the only limiting factor
questions.explanation: Only tube A provides all three required conditions: water, oxygen, and suitable warmth (20°C). B lacks water; C lacks oxygen (boiling removed dissolved O₂; oil prevents re-entry); D is too cold for enzyme activity.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of cross-pollination over self-pollination?
choices: It is faster and more reliable
It increases genetic variation in the offspring, making the population more adaptable to environmental change
It requires less energy from the plant
It produces seeds that germinate more quickly
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination combines genetic material from two different plants, producing offspring with greater genetic variation. This variation is the raw material for natural selection and adaptation.

questions.stem: During puberty, which hormone is primarily responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics (voice deepening, facial hair, muscle growth)?
questions.explanation: Testosterone, produced by the testes, triggers the development of male secondary sexual characteristics during puberty.

questions.stem: Why does a sperm cell contain many mitochondria in its midpiece?
choices: To provide ATP energy for the tail to swim towards the egg
To help the sperm penetrate the egg's outer layer
questions.explanation: The midpiece of a sperm cell is packed with mitochondria that produce ATP through respiration. This energy powers the flagellum (tail), enabling the sperm to swim through the female reproductive tract to reach the egg.
